summary: Defines a proposed MIB for the PSTN/Internet Interworking (PINT) services architecture, so tools can manage the servers that let Internet users start telephone calls and services. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is a dashboard layout for checking on a system that lets web users place phone calls.

subtitle: SNMP counters for watching how well a service that starts phone calls from the Internet is performing.

tldr.problem: PINT services let Internet users request voice and fax services from the telephone network (PSTN), and operators and users worry about reliability and security, especially across several providers.
tldr.mechanism: The PINT MIB defines SNMP objects that count calls received, completed and disconnected, per service type and time period, for the server as a whole, each client, each user and each gateway.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators read-only performance statistics for PINT services, but it is not meant to manage the PINT network elements themselves.

today: RFC 3055 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its module revision, dated 1 February 2001, is the only one the RFC records.

sections.title: What the PINT MIB Is For
sections.content:
PINT services are described in RFC 3055 as an emerging set of Internet-based applications where voice (and fax) requests to the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) are carried over the Internet. RFC 2458 introduces the pre-standard PINT architecture and services.

This document defines a MIB (Management Information Base) for monitoring the performance of a PINT-based service. It holds details of the four basic PINT services and their statistics measured under various criteria. Its purpose is limited: it is not meant to manage the PINT networking elements, and host and network performance are not addressed.

The RFC is written for the SNMP Management Framework. The module is compliant with SMIv2, and a SMIv1 version can be produced through translation, except where objects are omitted because no translation is possible (use of Counter64).
sections.eli5: It is a list of things to count so that people running a make-a-phone-call-from-the-web service can tell how well it is working.

sections.title: Why Monitor PINT Services
sections.content:
Voice and fax requests traditionally start and end inside the PSTN, a network known for robust handling of requests in terms of availability and security. When requests start on the Internet, users and providers worry about reliable forwarding of call requests to the PINT gateway under various network conditions, user and host authentication, and secure handling of user information. Performance and security management matter more when PINT services cross multiple administrative domains or providers.

The MIB lists the parameters to monitor on a per-user, per-PINT-client, per-PINT-server and per-PINT-gateway basis. PINT services, their invocation methods and their security issues are discussed in RFC 2848.
sections.eli5: Phone calls from the web cross more hands than normal calls, so everyone wants a way to check that calls are reliable and that only the right people make them.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC lists several choices made when building the MIB.

  • The configuration table extends the Application MIB (RFC 2287) using the AUGMENTS construct. Server location and contact come from the standard sysLocation and sysContact, but a separate pintSysContact exists because the PINT administrator may differ from the system administrator.
  • Gateway connections are monitored from the PINT server and placed in a separate group, so agents that cannot implement them are not forced to, through the MODULE-COMPLIANCE clauses.
  • No traps are defined. Thresholds on counters can be set with the Remote Monitoring MIB. Example events are repeated login or authentication failures from one client or user, and nuisance calls, meaning repeated calls to a number from the same user within a period.
  • The client and user tables may be resource demanding for an agent, so a control mechanism or a sorted topN view could be designed.
  • The client is identified by a SnmpAdminString that may hold an address and/or a name, to keep the number of indices small and the format readable.
  • The user ID must be unique across PINT servers and gateways. One way is to append the client ID to the user ID, with the session ID being that value plus a timestamp.
sections.eli5: The designers kept the scoreboard small, did not add alarm bells, and let people use a standard tool for alarms. They also made sure each caller has a name nobody else shares.

sections.title: Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The module is pintMib, placed at { mib-2 93 }. It has three branches: pintServerConfig (configuration), pintServerMonitor (statistics) and pintMibConformance.

The configuration branch has pintReleaseNumber (the PINT protocol version supported), pintSysContact (the only read-write object), a table of installed PINT applications and a table of registered gateways.

The monitor branch has four statistics tables, all indexed by service type and statistics period. The global table has one entry per service type and period. The client table adds the client address as an index, the user table adds the user name (SIZE(0..64)), and the gateway table adds the gateway name. Each reports calls received, successful and disconnected, and the client, user and global tables break out disconnections by cause such as authorization failure, server problems, gateway problems or egress facility problems.

The two textual conventions are PintServiceType and PintPerfStatPeriod. The RFC warns that counters for the sinceReboot period can roll over, and that applications must account for that.
sections.eli5: There is one scoreboard for the whole server, and others for each caller, each user and each phone gateway. Each is split by kind of service and by how long a time it covers.

sections.title: Conformance and Groups
sections.content:
The module defines one compliance statement, pintMibCompliance, with two mandatory groups. pintMibConfigGroup collects the configuration objects, and pintMibMonitorGroup collects the monitoring counters. The module defines no notifications.

The revision history records a single revision, dated 1 February 2001, as the initial version published as RFC 3055.
sections.eli5: A product that claims to follow the MIB must provide both the settings list and the counters list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only one object has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write: pintSysContact. There are no read-create objects. The RFC says this object may be sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and that allowing SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can harm network operations.

Other objects may contain information that is sensitive from a business perspective, so even reading them may need to be controlled. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575), so that only legitimate principals can read or change objects.
sections.eli5: Only one setting on the scoreboard can be changed, but even the numbers are private business information, so access should be locked down to the right people.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: RFC 3055 says that all extensions to the values listed in this MIB must be made through Standards Action processes as defined in RFC 2434. The module's object identifier is placed under mib-2 as number 93.
sections.eli5: Nobody may add new kinds of count to the list without going through the official standards process.

items.label: sinceReboot
items.desc: Since the PINT server was last rebooted; may roll over.
